body:
Why the Ocean Has a Temperature Gradient

Sunlight warms the upper layers of tropical oceans, while deeper seawater remains comparatively cold. This creates a temperature gradient, meaning the change in temperature per unit distance between 2 regions.

Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) uses the temperature difference between warm surface seawater and cold deep seawater to produce useful energy. Unlike tidal energy, OTEC does not depend on the gravitational rise and fall of sea level. Unlike wave energy, it does not depend directly on the motion of wind-generated waves.

OTEC is most promising where warm surface water is available close to deep cold water, particularly in tropical ocean regions and around some islands. A substantial and relatively persistent temperature difference, commonly around 20°C or greater, is desirable for practical electricity generation.

How OTEC Produces Electricity

Because the temperature difference is relatively small compared with that used in many conventional thermal power plants, OTEC requires suitable heat-transfer arrangements and has important efficiency limitations.

Closed-Cycle OTEC

In a closed-cycle OTEC system, warm surface seawater transfers heat to a separate fluid with a low boiling point, such as ammonia. That fluid vaporises and drives a turbine. Cold deep seawater then removes heat from the vapour, causing it to condense. The working fluid circulates within its own closed circuit.

Open-Cycle OTEC

In an open-cycle OTEC system, warm seawater is exposed to sufficiently low pressure so that some of it evaporates. The resulting water vapour can drive a suitable turbine. When the vapour is condensed using cold deep seawater, it can provide freshwater because the dissolved salts remain behind during evaporation.

Thus, both open-cycle and closed-cycle OTEC use the same ocean temperature difference, but the fluid passing through the power-generating cycle differs.

Ocean Thermal Desalination Is a Related but Distinct Application

Cold deep seawater can also support low-temperature thermal desalination (LTTD). This technology uses a temperature difference and low-pressure evaporation and condensation to produce freshwater. A desalination facility does not automatically generate electricity simply because it uses ocean thermal resources.

The distinction matters when considering Indian projects. The National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) has worked on ocean-based desalination and ocean-energy applications.

India's Lakshadweep Connection

A Ministry of Earth Sciences announcement dated 7 March 2026 stated that NIOT-supported LTTD plants were operational on 8 islands of Lakshadweep. The announcement separately described an OTEC-powered desalination facility at Kavaratti as being developed, with construction and installation work in progress.

Accordingly, the March 2026 evidence supports 2 different statements: operational LTTD desalination existed on 8 islands, while the Kavaratti OTEC-powered desalination project was under development. The latter should not be described as already commissioned on the basis of that announcement.

Environmental and Site Constraints

OTEC requires access to large quantities of seawater at different temperatures, and this is difficult where deep cold water is far offshore. Moving seawater through an installation can affect marine organisms. Discharge temperature, mixing, nutrient redistribution and working-fluid safety also require attention.

Its resource is relatively steady in suitable tropical regions, but technological and site constraints have limited widespread commercial deployment.

Salinity-Gradient Energy

Salinity-gradient energy uses the difference in salt concentration between freshwater and seawater, such as where rivers enter the sea. This chemical potential can be converted into useful energy through technologies involving selective membranes or other controlled mixing processes.

Salinity-gradient energy is different from OTEC: it exploits a difference in salt concentration, not temperature. It is also different from tidal energy because it does not rely on periodic sea-level changes. Practical development remains at relatively early stages compared with established renewable technologies.

Prelims focus

  • OTEC uses warm surface seawater and cold deep seawater.
  • A substantial temperature difference, commonly around 20°C or greater, is desirable for practical OTEC electricity generation.
  • Closed-cycle OTEC uses a separate low-boiling working fluid.
  • Open-cycle OTEC evaporates seawater at low pressure and can produce freshwater upon condensation.
  • As reported on 7 March 2026, LTTD plants operated on 8 Lakshadweep islands, while the Kavaratti OTEC-powered facility remained under development.
  • Trap: Salinity-gradient energy uses salt-concentration differences; OTEC uses temperature differences.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, 'Marine Energy Glossary', section 'Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion', accessed 16 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Report to Congress on Potential Environmental Effects of Marine and Hydrokinetic Energy', section 2.3, 'Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion'; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Press Information Bureau release on ocean-based desalination projects in Lakshadweep, 7 March 2026.]

body:
Identify the Resource Before Identifying the Technology

The most reliable way to distinguish these renewable-energy technologies is to identify the natural resource supplying the energy. A turbine may be present in a geothermal, tidal, wave or OTEC system, but the presence of a turbine does not establish which resource is being used.

Similarly, biological feedstocks may yield gas, liquid fuel, heat or electricity. The energy pathway must be identified from the feedstock and conversion process rather than only from the final product.

Core Resource Comparison

TechnologyPrimary resourcePrincipal constraint
Biomass combustionCombustible biological materialSustainable feedstock supply and air pollution
BiogasSuitable biodegradable organic matterDigester operation, contamination and methane leakage
Liquid biofuelsSugars, starches, oils or processed residuesFeedstock sustainability and lifecycle emissions
GeothermalUnderground heatSuitable geological resource and access
TidalTidal water movement or height differenceAppropriate coastal geography and tidal conditions
WaveWind-generated surface wavesWave climate and equipment durability
OTECSurface-to-deep seawater temperature differenceWarm surface water and accessible cold deep water
Salinity-gradient energyFreshwater–seawater salinity differenceSuitable mixing locations and developing technology

Predictability and Controllability Are Different

Predictability refers to how accurately future resource availability can be forecast. Controllability refers to how far operators can choose when usable energy is produced.

Tidal conditions can be predicted accurately, but the available energy changes during the tidal cycle. A biomass plant can use stored fuel to produce energy at chosen times, but this requires a dependable feedstock supply. Suitable geothermal resources can provide relatively steady heat. Wave-energy output varies with changing sea conditions, while tropical ocean thermal gradients may be more persistent.

None of these general characteristics removes the need for site-specific assessment. A poorly located plant may perform badly even when its technology is sound.

Commercial Maturity Must Be Considered Separately from Resource Potential

Biomass combustion, conventional biogas systems and ethanol production are established technologies. Conventional geothermal electricity generation is commercially established in several countries, although India's geothermal power development remained largely exploratory and demonstrative in the government information available on 2 November 2026.

Some tidal-range systems have operated commercially, while tidal-stream technologies continue to develop. Wave energy and OTEC have had research and demonstration applications, but widespread commercial deployment remains limited. Salinity-gradient electricity technologies are still comparatively immature.

A large theoretical resource does not imply that equally large capacity can be built economically, environmentally or technologically. Resource estimates, technical potential, planned projects, projects under construction and operating capacity are separate categories.

India and Gujarat: One-Glance Location Associations

  • Gujarat tidal resources: Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Gujarat geothermal resource: Cambay Graben.
  • Indian geothermal exploration: Puga Valley in Ladakh.
  • Indian ocean thermal applications: NIOT work in Lakshadweep, including LTTD desalination and development of the Kavaratti OTEC-powered facility.
  • Biomass applications: Agricultural residues, livestock waste, sugar-processing residues and suitable segregated organic wastes.

Environmental Assessment Across Technologies

Each resource has a different main environmental concern. Biomass raises questions about land, soil nutrients, air pollution and lifecycle emissions. Biogas requires control of methane leakage and safe digestate use. Geothermal development needs responsible management of underground fluids, gases and reservoir conditions. Marine installations require attention to habitats, water movement, fisheries and coastal or ocean ecosystems.

These differences explain why no single renewable technology is automatically appropriate for every location. The best use depends on the resource, technology maturity, environmental safeguards and local needs.

Prelims focus

  • Biomass is a chemical-energy resource; geothermal energy is a heat resource.
  • Tidal-range generation uses water-level differences; tidal-stream generation uses moving water.
  • Wave energy mainly uses wind-generated waves; OTEC uses a temperature difference.
  • Biogas is produced biologically without oxygen; gasification is a high-temperature conversion process.
  • Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kachchh are associated with tidal potential; Cambay Graben is associated with geothermal potential.
  • Trap: Resource potential, a proposed project and an operating power plant are not interchangeable facts.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed pp. 33–36; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 'Water', printed pp. 33–36; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Geothermal Basics' and 'Marine Energy Basics', accessed 16 November 2026; MNRE, Press Information Bureau announcement on ocean energy, 22 August 2019; Press Information Bureau, 'Geothermal Energy: A New Chapter in India's Clean Energy Journey', 2 November 2026; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Press Information Bureau release on Lakshadweep desalination projects, 7 March 2026.]
